lessons.title: Numbers 13 to 17

grammar.title: Numbers 13 to 17
grammar.explanation: Numbers from 13 to 17 end in -teen. Say the -teen part clearly so the number is easy to hear.
examples: My brother is thirteen years old.

Use 'forty' for 40; notice it is spelled f-o-r-t-y without a u.
Say 'fifty' for 50, halfway to one hundred.

grammar.title: -teen vs. -ty
grammar.explanation: Numbers 13 to 19 end in -teen. Tens like twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty end in -ty.

lessons.title: How much is it?
lessons.scenario: Ben visits Smarty's shop and asks about the price of a hat and a coat.

items.example: I like this hat. How much is it?
items.note: Ask 'How much is it?' when you want to know the price of something.
Use 'money' for the coins and paper bills you use to buy things.

image.describe: shiny gold coins and folded green paper bills resting on a shop counter

items.note: Say 'dollar' for one, and 'dollars' for two or more.

image.describe: a crisp green paper banknote with a star emblem in the center

items.note: Call something 'cheap' when the price is low.

items.example: This coat is ninety dollars. It is expensive!
items.note: Say 'expensive' when something costs a lot of money.

grammar.title: Asking the price
grammar.explanation: Ask 'How much is it?' for one item, and answer with 'It is' plus the number of dollars.

practice.prompt: You want to know the price of a shirt. What do you ask?
practice.explanation: Ask 'How much is it?' to find out the price.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.

practice.explanation: A low price is cheap, and a high price is expensive.

practice.explanation: Expensive means it costs a lot of money.

practice.text: This pen is one dollar. It is ___.
practice.explanation: Use cheap when the price is low.

practice.prompt: Ask and answer about the price aloud.
practice.text: How much is it? It is thirty dollars.
practice.answer: How much is it? It is thirty dollars.
practice.explanation: Ask 'How much is it?' and answer with the price in dollars.

items.note: A 'market' is a busy place where people buy fresh food.

image.describe: an outdoor market stall piled with baskets of red apples, yellow bananas, and orange carrots under a striped awning

items.note: Use 'kilo' when you weigh food like rice, cheese, or fruit.

items.note: Ask 'How many' when you want to count things like kilos or bottles.

image.describe: a clear glass bottle filled with fresh cold water

items.example: I would like two bottles of milk, please.
items.note: Say 'I would like' as a polite way to ask for something.

grammar.title: How much vs. How many
grammar.explanation: Use 'How much' for prices and things you cannot count. Use 'How many' for things you can count, like kilos and bottles.
examples: How many bottles of water do you want?

episode.title: The Blue Box at the Market

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: Smarty is in his shop. He has one hundred dollars in cash!

image.describe: Smarty the black cat smiling proudly beside a neat stack of cash on his shop counter.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: Hello, Smarty! Can I help you?

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: Yes, Mia! We can go to the market.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: I would like two kilos of rice and three bottles of juice.

image.describe: Mia the cat pointing to bags of rice and bottles of orange juice at a colorful outdoor market stall.

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: How much is it? It is twenty five dollars.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: Smarty! There is a small blue box under that table!

panels.speaker: Smarty
panels.text: Whose is this box? There is a key next to it!

image.describe: Smarty the black cat and Mia the cat peering under a wooden market table at a small blue box with a shiny brass key beside it.

panels.speaker: Mia
panels.text: A key and a box! What is in the box?
